title: Integrated Circuits, AI, and Wallabies
subtitle: Two very different essays written while waiting for doctors
contentHtml:
Most of my medical issues are now in the clear, with one last issue to resolve. For the last several weeks I’ve been being poked, scanned, and imaged, with the net result that I’ve been put on blood thinners (probably for the rest of my life) and advised to stay in the country until December.

I’ve been using the down time to read, walk, and think about what I want to do when I do finally get a green light, and where to take this newsletter, which is now almost five years old.

When I realized I couldn’t go overseas I began to think of focusing on Northern California and the Pacific Northwest, the part of the country I know the least, but what I’ve seen I love. In particular I began exploring a long walk in the Bay Area, from San Jose to San Francisco, which after a lot of feedback, became this walk1.

While researching I ended up reading books on the birth of the integrated circuit, and consequently the modern technological age as we know it2.

The project that emerged is to explore the beginning of the computer age, as viewed through the invention of the transistor, and then the production of the integrated circuit, and what impact that has had on the world, not just economically. Or what does it mean to live in the age of high-tech machines, at the human level?

No technology has changed the world as irrevocably as the solid-state transistor did, which after its invention in 1947 unleashed seventy-five years of innovation that altered how we live, and more importantly, how we think. With it, we have built electronic brains, crafted from silicon, phosphorus, boron, silicon dioxide, copper, and many other raw elements — initially focused on replicating repetitive tasks, but over time we’ve climbed the tower of capability into air so rarefied it’s threatening to go beyond the human.

While that change began in the US, centered in the Bay Area, it’s now global, and to be alive in 2026 means to be formed by, and to live in, a world of machines crafted by the transistor.

There are obvious parallels here to the current issues around AI — which continues this story while also being an invention in its own right. To use a term appropriate to the subject, AI is a phase transition into a different environment, where continuity can no longer be assumed. While the transistor set off immense disruption, the path followed after has generally been knowable and predictable, as Moore’s Law suggests, and constrained by being grounded in human thought. AI is a transition into a different realm.

To simplify, the transistor revolution unfolded through a succession of inventions which sprung from the minds of humans. AI threatens to break that relationship, because it threatens how we think — it is no longer direct human thought — and so we may be entering a period in which the pace of change, and the type of change, may outrun our ability to understand what’s going on, and so we completely misjudge the consequences. We risk entering an age of Techne3 without any Metis — technology advancing without practical wisdom to bound it.

Not that we did much better last time. One of the parallels that struck me while reading the history of the integrated circuit was that even though it came from human minds, there was a relative lack of introspection, or coordination. The rise of the age of integrated circuits and computers was a change so constitutive, accomplished so quickly, and yet done with little thought to what it all might mean. Sure there were those who worried about the impact of such a fundamental change, about a loss of innocence, about the technology falling into the wrong hands, about economic disruption, but that did almost nothing to stop it from happening, or how it evolved. It also happened not because any single person, government, or interest alone, mandated that it should be so, but because man innovates, driven by a desire for power (military), safety (military and public), knowledge (academics), and comfort (public) the way a beaver builds a dam.

What does this all have to do with walking? While reading I was thinking about what was not in the books, which was what was taking place outside of the towers, laboratories, and clean-rooms. The architecture of daily life might be very different now than it was in 1947, but people still pray at altars, still mourn death, still lose themselves in someone else, still wonder why they are here, and in each nation they do it differently, in ways they did two hundred years ago. The Techne might have won; but the Metis persists, bubbling and gurgling beneath it, a messy mass of emotional irrationality that can never be eliminated.

I’ve seen that in my own life, as has anyone my age or older who grew up in a world without home computers, smart phones, and the internet, and knows that while things are very different now, they are not that different. I remember when I saw my first computer, a TRS-80 that showed up one day in Miss K’s math class in 1979, a boxy contraption with phosphor green text, chunky keys, and an attached tape player as memory. I received special approval to stay after school for two hours each day, to learn to program it, and after a week I’d written a program that flashed “Hello Ace” on the screen in a sequence determined by what song you chose.

Thinking back to that moment, almost all the promises made then — regular space flight, cures for diseases, inordinately materially richer and more comfortable lives — have been met and vastly exceeded and yet I’m struck by what hasn’t changed. Sitting here typing this in a McDonald’s, watching a young father help his excited toddler decide which Happy Meal toy to get, families coming in from church, elderly men complaining about being old, I still feel I am a human living in a very human world.

Maybe I’m being naive about what AI will do to us, because while I am certain there will be a great deal of disruption, much of it painful, I’m still optimistic about the human capacity to endure, and thrive, even if our technology outruns our Metis. I don’t see the world ending, nor do I see it being eroded to a substrate devoid of spirituality. The transcendent is the carpet too big for the room. We can push the bump down with the collective weight of billions of silicon wafers, or extensive physical networks of electrical networks, but it will simply pop up somewhere else, different but still recognizable. I suppose I have that much faith in the Metis.

But back to my project on the transistor, which is to follow the path of it from an idea, to physical object, to industrial process, to epoch-transforming technology, and finally to the invisible constituent parts of ordinary modern life.

At each stop I want to focus less on the engineering, physics, and economics, and more on ordinary life, because while invention is our age’s telos, the human condition cannot be reduced to precise configurations of electrons on silicon, and no mechanical disruption, no matter how transformational, can erode the enchantment of living.

Here are the more important steps I’ve identified, and what I think is interesting about each. Of course what you find when you walk is always different than what you expect, and if I end up doing this I’m sure I’ll come away with some very different conclusions. Maybe even a realization that we have reached a point at which the Metis is endangered. I doubt that, but again, that’s why I walk.

Step 0 — Birth of Transistor (Murray Hill, NJ) — Bell Labs, where it all began, and the quantum physics that led up to it. Exploration of America as land of intellectual manifest destiny, drawing from a pool of scientific and engineering ingenuity from every state, and many different nations.

Step 1 — Materials needed (Spruce Pine, NC, Congo and/or Australia, Mongolia) — Mined high-purity quartz rock and cobalt are the building blocks. The cobalt currently comes mostly from Congo, but could come from Australia, but that requires higher labor cost (less exploitation) and overcoming environmental opposition. Mining in Mongolia has become its largest export industry, with materials crucial in production of integrated circuits (copper, lanthanum, and neodymium and praseodymium for EUV machines), and that has changed the country, bringing it into the advanced world, changing how they live. The horse replaced by high-tech Priuses, and the steppe by the Ger slums that ring Ulaanbaatar.

Step 2 — Chip blueprints (SF Bay Area): Where the modern integrated circuit became a reality. Stanford Industrial Park, Fairchild, Intel, NVIDIA, AMD, and so many others. Also, Moffett Field, because NASA (and military) was essential to success of early industry. Apollo and Minuteman II provided crucial early markets for integrated circuits, with buyers willing to pay well above market. More on American exceptionalism.

Step 3 — Silicon Wafer production (Japan): Why are silicon wafers crafted in Japan? Combination of prior optics industry, and a postwar industrial policy decision of Japanese government (MITI). Not just Tokyo, but production all across Japan. Companies include Shin-Etsu, Sumco (Kyushu), and JSR (Tokyo) for specialized chemicals. Japan as follower, not leader.

Step 4 — Equipment for production (Netherlands / Germany): Perhaps most fascinating step because machines used to print circuits are themselves extraordinary technology, so much so that the Dutch company that makes most of them basically has a monopoly: Those are the ASML EUV lithography machines in Veldhoven, which use another singular product — Carl Zeiss precision mirrors from Oberkochen. A continuation of the Dutch as an engineering society (built on drained land), and Germans as precise manufacturers.

Step 5 — Fabrication of Logic Chips (Taiwan): How did Taiwan become location for fabrication of majority of logic chips, in particular one company in one city — TSMC in Hsinchu. Once again through centralized government planning (ITRI), and then because of one man, Morris Chang from Texas Instruments. National industrial policy, as much as free markets, is the central actor here. Focus on the large traditional shrines around the plants, built with money from the industry.

Step 6 — Fabrication of DRAM and NAND flash Memory chips (South Korea): Samsung in Hwaseong, SK Hynix in Icheon. Where Taiwan’s story is mostly government planning, South Korea’s is mostly Samsung’s chairman Lee Byung-chul making a substantial bet that Korea could beat Japan at memory chips — at the time a seemingly reckless bet fueled by national animosity, a centuries-long sense of inferiority, that ended up being a huge winner.

Step 7 — Packaging and testing (Malaysia): Again, why do a different step in a different location? In this case precision testing, by Intel, ASE Group, and Amkor Technology — largely story of company looking for inexpensive labor, which then brings about benefits of conglomeration, including a highly skilled labor force. A good example of how what starts as exploitation often ends with the exploited benefiting more — a poor nation becomes a prosperous one. A third world nation starts its journey to a first world nation. Is exploitation worth it? Clearly not a question with a simple answer.

Step 8 — PCB manufacturing and device assembly (China): The last, and least technologically advanced step, which is putting it all together, either via printed circuit boards in Shenzhen and Dongguan, or assembling iPhones in Zhengzhou. China trying to move up the food chain, but lots of global pressure to keep them in the “dark.” Adds significant fuel to the politics of Taiwan versus China. To be blunt, China is jealous.

Step 9 — Distribution (China / Global): Cargo from Shanghai Airport or port to malls, shops, and warehouses in every city, village, and neighborhood across the globe.

I’ve been to many of these places, so I know most of this project is doable, but I don’t know if I will get around to doing all of this, or even most of it, but a man can dream. Regardless, I do believe the best way to try and understand what is coming with AI is to know what came from the last technological revolution, and that means understanding the integrated circuit industry.

Kangaroos finally! Or at least Wallabies

When I first went to Australia I expected to see plenty of kangaroos. I was certain of that because of what the country told me through its books, movies, TV shows, and iconography, including the tail of the airplane I was on, where a fifteen-foot white roo was symbolically leaping us across the ocean, into the land of his species.

I wasn’t entirely naive, didn’t entirely buy the marketing. I didn’t expect kangaroos to be hopping around downtown Sydney, sitting next to me at cafes sipping coffee, but I did expect to see them munching on grass in suburbs, or sitting next to roads waiting to cross, akin to deer in the US.

So I was a little miffed for my first two weeks when I saw none, not on the golf courses, not in the vast parks I walked through, or the empty fields in the outer suburbs. But I was certainly going to see them when I went to Townsville, a smaller, less developed city, and then I would get to experience whole mobs of them during my twenty-seven-hour bus ride to Alice Springs in the center of the outback.

But I didn’t see any in Townsville, not even up in the rocky hills around it, neither did I see any saltwater crocodiles, or sharks, although the signs strung along the beach every fifty yards saying to beware of them, as well as the bottles of vinegar to splash on a jellyfish sting to keep it from being fatal (“within three minutes.”) did illustrate why Australia has elevated the kangaroo to its mascot — in a country of such belligerent flora and fauna, go with the cute, less murderous one.

I’d resigned myself to a roo-free urban experience, but as I stepped on the Greyhound I was excited because I would certainly see them bounding across the outback, as well as their carcasses littering the roadside. The last bit I was promised by plenty of Australians, who told me with a twisted pride, and in gory details I didn’t relish. “Mate, they are pests. Can take out a whole car. They will splatter like a bag of blood and guts across the windshield of your bus.”

Yet for twenty-seven hours I saw nothing alive bigger than a single house cat, a rail-thin creature with a snake hanging out of its mouth, walking through a denuded landscape of red soil spotted with scrub brush and termite mounds. Where were the unending vistas with kangaroos bounding beside my bus, their silhouettes against a swollen red setting sun, like a feral real-world version of the tail of my Qantas plane? Where was the antipodean version of bison roaming the great plains I’d been promised? While we’d genocided our great herds, eliminating them for cattle, Australia hadn’t done that, because the land was too harsh and sparse to farm, so where were they? Hiding from me I presumed.

When I didn’t see any in Alice Springs, or in Melbourne, or again in Sydney, even though I’d turned it into a bit and three readers took me specifically to see kangaroos, and somehow we didn’t see them, I felt cheated, and left Australia joking that I wanted my money back.

I’ll admit some of it was self-inflicted, because I did turn down trips to kangaroo sanctuaries, but that was cheating. I wanted to see them in the wild, feral, not presented to me for a fee, like strippers.

This trip I came in with zero expectations, which were met for the first three weeks. I saw no kangaroos in Perth, or on my twenty-four-hour bus ride from Darwin to Alice Springs, although again I heard about how often they splatter on windshields. This time it was at a rest stop in Birdum4, where I’d mistakenly mentioned I’d hoped I’d see a kangaroo, and that set off a round of bragging by the bus driver and a table of truckers, all in high-vis vests, shorts, and flip-flops, but otherwise exactly the same types you would find at a Love’s in Missouri. It became one of those “I can outdo you” conversations, but about killing kangaroos and wallabies, with lots of diminutives (brekkie, choccy biccy, pokies, etc.), and visceral carnage. Men can sure turn anything into a competition5.

Then, on my third day in Alice Springs, while beginning my daily five-mile walk through the countryside, I finally saw one. A beige wallaby sitting high up on beige rock on a hillside of beige rocks surrounded by beige brush. I stopped and stared, excited as a child, and then I spotted more of them, all hopping around from rock to rock, like stuffed animals come to life. I was on a trail peering up, which made others stop to look at what I was looking at, and all the locals stopped, expecting to see something dramatic, like a fire or a person in distress, but it was only a ten-a-penny wallaby so they moved on, no doubt chuckling to themselves about that silly American. One French couple joined me, also entranced, whipped out their phones and took every form of selfie-with-wallaby imaginable. Then an Aboriginal man, who I’d regularly exchange good mornings and afternoons with, came up and began to tell me about how you can catch them and eat them, not here, mind you, but out in the bush.

For the next few days I stopped at this hillside often and gawked at the cluster of wallabies, overjoyed, childlike. It was truly magical and it is a highlight of my five years of travels. I’m sure to Australians that sounds close to unimaginable, but there is something so fanciful and special about a country so similar, but populated with entirely different creatures. As if you woke from a dream and a little of its absurdity never left.

I didn’t see wallabies anywhere other than that one outcrop, not even on my long walk through the surrounding countryside, or any kangaroos ever, but when I got back to Sydney I did see whales.

It was during my daily walk along the coastline, near Malabar Beach, where I spotted over ten migrating humpbacks, including a mother with her young calf. I don’t have any photos, or great videos, because I was content to just watch, and listen, because they got close enough I could hear them.

For all the words I’ve written about Australia, all the supposedly deep thoughts, these are the two images from my two trips that I will never forget — the wallaby and the migrating whales.

You can dress up travel in fancy language, justify it with erudite essays (and I sure have), but the only reason you need is the childlike joy that comes with being somewhere different.

If you ever lose that sense of wonder, then stop traveling. Thanks, Mr. Wallaby, for reminding me I still have it.

PS: I don’t know exactly when I will be able to travel again, hopefully within a month, at least in the US. If I get the clearance for that, then my next trip will be to the Bay Area, to try and do the walk from Richmond to San Jose. I’ll post dates/details before, because I would love company, and I know a lot of readers are in the area and know a lot more about high-tech than I do!

1

As I wrote last week —

Why focus on the east side rather than a walk from San Francisco to San Jose via Palo Alto? I think there is more going on that interests me on that side -- from the Kaiser shipyard that brought an influx of workers during WW2, to the de-industrialization of the 60s/70s that produced modern Oakland, to the post-war high-tech boom (admittedly centered across the bay on the west side) that created a wealthy/suburban Fremont, to recent immigration (drawn by high-tech work), all overlaid on a ranching/Spanish past, it’s more on the east, or at least in an in-your-face way, than on the west. As well as the Spanish Missions, specifically Mission San José in Fremont.

2

Books I’ve been reading: The Idea Factory by Jon Gertner, The Chip by T.R. Reid, The Man Behind the Microchip by Leslie Berlin, Chip War by Chris Miller, and even my forty-year-old copy of Quantum Physics by Eisberg and Resnick, which was one of the seminal texts for us graduate students (the other was The Feynman Lectures on Physics) who were told “to pass the oral exams solve every problem in it”, which is what I did. For six months we all carried it around everywhere, tattered and taped up. Given the role it took in our lives, as something we had to navigate to get a PhD, or crash out, we ended up calling it Iceberg and Titanic — “Hey, how did you solve those last five problems in the solid-state chapter of Iceberg and Titanic?”

3

Techne and Metis are fancy words popularized by James C. Scott for scientific knowledge versus common sense. Or top-down book learning, versus bottom-up intuitive learning. I like this framework because it captures a lot of the differences I see in how people think, and how societies are run. One definition I’ve seen is:

  • Techne is technical, scientific, and formal knowledge. It describes methods, procedures, and rules that can be systematically learned and applied. It tends to be codified, explicit, formal, standardized, top-down, abstracted, generalized, and universally applicable.

  • Metis is practical, experiential, tacit knowledge. It’s the accumulated wisdom or know-how that comes from practice or lived experience.

4

Birdum is a region with sixty-three residents and a petrol station. I figured the name was another Australian toddler-ization, given because there were a lot of birds there or something, but no, it was apparently the nickname the surveyor in 1870 called his wife, so that’s what he called the only notable landmark around, the creek that passes near. I don’t want to know why a lonely man in the outback calls a creek the same loving name he calls his wife. Just don’t want to know.

5

There is something quaint about the casual brutality, dark humor, and practicality of Australians in the outback, especially because it comes with such joviality. They have little of the bitterness of the US working class, or the cynical fatalism of the English. The Australian working class (sorry, Aussie tradies), including truckers (truckies), are such a sunny lot — gregarious, optimistic, and cheerfully irreverent, even when complaining. They even have their own word for it, larrikin, which evolved from “An unruly or violent youth” to “A mischievous, boisterous, or frolicsome person who is characterized by good-natured irreverence and a disregard for convention.”
